findings.title: Production auth filter uses Optional.get()
findings.description: The tech-lead prohibited checklist flags Optional.get() usage in production code. This instance is guarded by isEmpty(), so the immediate runtime risk is low, but it still violates the repository standard and creates a pattern future maintainers may copy less safely.
findings.evidence:
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken authentication = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
					user.get(),
					token,
					List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + user.get().role())));
findings.suggestedFix: Assign the validated principal without Optional.get(), for example: AdminUserDto adminUser = adminAuthUseCase.validateToken(token).orElse(null); then handle null before constructing the Authentication.

findings.title: Docker profile has a hard-coded database password default
findings.description: The Docker profile falls back to a committed password value. Even if intended only for local demo use, the AGENTS security standard prohibits hard-coded passwords/secrets in source-controlled configuration, and OSS users can accidentally deploy defaults unchanged.
findings.evidence: password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the password default from application-docker.yml and provide a non-secret .env.example or docker-compose sample that developers must explicitly copy/configure.

findings.title: Zero-hit priority thresholds are duplicated in three layers
findings.description: Priority calculation exists in ZeroHitPriorityDecider, ZeroHitSearch.priorityFor(), and the PostgreSQL upsert SQL CASE expression. This splits one business rule across domain, entity, and infrastructure code; changing thresholds later can silently create divergent persisted rows or entity restore failures.
findings.evidence: ZeroHitPriorityDecider decides HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW at src/main/java/com/skishop/domain/ZeroHitPriorityDecider.java:19, the entity repeats it here, and ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway repeats it in SQL at lines 52-56.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the domain policy the single Java source of truth and isolate the SQL duplication behind clearly named constants/tests, or move the invariant so entity restoration does not encode an independent threshold table.

findings.title: Repository/infrastructure gateway is placed in the service package
findings.description: ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway is annotated as @Repository and owns native SQL/JdbcTemplate access, but it lives under com.skishop.service. That blurs the designed Controller -> Service -> Repository/Infrastructure separation and makes package ownership less obvious for future maintainers.
findings.evidence:
@Repository
public class ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway {
findings.suggestedFix: Move the gateway to a repository or infrastructure package and inject it into ZeroHitRecordingService through a small interface if needed.

findings.title: JaCoCo coverage target is not enforced
findings.description: AGENTS requires at least 80% line and branch coverage or documented exceptions. The Maven config only prepares the agent and generates a report; it does not configure jacoco:check thresholds, so the build can pass below the required coverage target.
findings.evidence: The jacoco-maven-plugin executions include prepare-agent and report only; no check execution or 0.80 line/branch limits are configured.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a jacoco:check execution with LINE and BRANCH minimums of 0.80, or add documented exceptions explaining why the target cannot currently be met.

findings.title: Repository implementation is placed in the service package
findings.description: `ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway` is annotated with `@Repository`, owns SQL/JDBC access, and injects a repository, but it is declared under `com.skishop.service`. This mixes persistence infrastructure into the service package and weakens the service/repository boundary.
findings.evidence: Line 1 declares `package com.skishop.service;`; line 20 declares `@Repository`; lines 25-57 contain the PostgreSQL upsert SQL.
findings.suggestedFix: Move this class to `com.skishop.repository` or a clearly defined infrastructure/persistence package, then inject it into `ZeroHitRecordingService` from that boundary.

findings.title: API DTO depends on a persistence-layer enum
findings.description: `ZeroHitItemDto` imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority` and exposes it as a response field. Even though this is not a JPA entity class, it leaks a persistence package type into the API contract and couples frontend JSON semantics to the entity layer.
findings.evidence: Line 3 imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority`; line 17 exposes `Priority priority` in the DTO record.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose a DTO/API enum or a stable string field, and map from the entity enum in `ZeroHitMapper`. Keep entity package types inside service/repository/model boundaries.

findings.title: JPA entities are not in the required model package
findings.description: The architecture checklist requires JPA entities under `com.skishop.model`, but the implementation uses `com.skishop.entity`. This is a package convention deviation and causes downstream imports from repository/domain/service/dto to depend on `entity` instead of the expected model boundary.
findings.evidence: `Product.java` declares `package com.skishop.entity;` and `@Entity`. `ZeroHitSearch.java` follows the same pattern at lines 1 and 19.
findings.suggestedFix: Either move JPA classes/enums to `com.skishop.model` and update imports, or update the authoritative architecture standard if `entity` is the intended package name.

findings.title: Request and response DTOs are not separated
findings.description: The architecture checklist expects `dto/request` and `dto/response` packages. The implementation keeps request DTOs, response DTOs, and shared DTOs flat under `com.skishop.dto`, making the API direction less explicit as the contract grows.
findings.evidence: `AiConsultRequest.java` declares `package com.skishop.dto;`; response DTOs such as `AiConsultResponse.java` also declare the same flat package.
findings.suggestedFix: Move request payload records such as `LoginRequest` and `AiConsultRequest` into `com.skishop.dto.request`, and response records into `com.skishop.dto.response`. Keep shared value DTOs only if deliberately documented.

findings.title: Development and production profile separation is missing
findings.description: Only `application.yml` and `application-docker.yml` exist under main resources. The checklist expects common, development, and production profile separation; current common config also contains localhost-oriented defaults for datasource and CORS.
findings.evidence: Line 14 defaults the datasource URL to localhost; line 57 defaults CORS to `http://localhost:3000`. Main resources contain `application.yml` and `application-docker.yml`, but no `application-dev.yml` or `application-prod.yml`.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep shared defaults in `application.yml`, move local developer defaults to `application-dev.yml`, and add production-safe `application-prod.yml` requiring explicit datasource/CORS/admin settings.

findings.title: Client IP extraction is implemented inside the authentication controller
findings.description: `AuthController` contains header parsing and fallback logic for `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, and remote address. This is cross-cutting request metadata handling inside a controller method helper rather than a filter, resolver, or dedicated request-context component.
findings.evidence: Lines 60-69 parse forwarding headers and return the client IP used by the login limiter.
findings.suggestedFix: Move client IP resolution to a request metadata component, `HandlerMethodArgumentResolver`, or servlet filter, then pass a resolved value into the use case.

findings.title: PostgreSQL upsert mutates aggregate state and duplicates domain rules outside the aggregate
findings.description: ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway writes hit_count, priority, estimated_opportunity_loss, and timestamps directly with SQL. This bypasses ZeroHitSearch.firstHit()/recordRepeat() and repeats the priority/opportunity-loss rules in infrastructure, so aggregate invariants can drift between the JPA fallback path and PostgreSQL path.
findings.evidence: UPSERT_SQL sets hit_count, estimated_opportunity_loss, and priority with CASE thresholds directly in SQL; upsert() executes it at lines 96-102.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep concurrent safety inside a repository implementation, but load/lock the aggregate and invoke ZeroHitSearch.firstHit()/recordRepeat(), or otherwise centralize all priority/loss calculation behind one domain policy used by every persistence path. Add regression tests proving PostgreSQL and fallback paths cannot diverge.

findings.title: Money concepts are modeled as raw BigDecimal fields instead of immutable value objects
findings.description: Product.price and ZeroHitSearch.estimatedOpportunityLoss are monetary domain concepts but are stored directly as BigDecimal. The DDD checklist requires value objects such as Money to be immutable records with self-validation and explicit persistence mapping.
findings.evidence: Product declares private BigDecimal price; ZeroHitSearch similarly declares private BigDecimal estimatedOpportunityLoss at src/main/java/com/skishop/entity/ZeroHitSearch.java:40-41.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce a Money or OpportunityLoss value object with non-negative validation, currency/scale rules as appropriate, and @Embedded/@Embeddable or an AttributeConverter for persistence. Keep BigDecimal only at DTO/API boundaries if that is the public contract.

findings.title: Product search directly records zero-hit demand instead of publishing a domain event
findings.description: ProductSearchService directly depends on ZeroHitRecordingService and calls record() inside the search transaction when totalCount is zero. No ApplicationEventPublisher, domain event record, @EventListener, or @TransactionalEventListener exists in main code, so inter-aggregate coordination is tightly coupled.
findings.evidence: ProductSearchService injects ZeroHitRecordingService at lines 24-32 and calls zeroHitRecordingService.record(trimmedKeyword) at line 64; repository-wide search found no ApplicationEventPublisher or transactional event listener usage.
findings.suggestedFix: Publish a past-tense event such as ProductSearchReturnedNoResultsEvent from the search use case, then handle it in a zero-hit event handler within an appropriate transaction phase to record demand. Keep the event payload minimal: keyword, category/sort context if needed, result count, and occurredAt.

findings.title: Zero-hit priority thresholds have multiple authoritative implementations
findings.description: Priority is calculated in ZeroHitSearch.priorityFor(), ZeroHitPriorityDecider.decide(), and the PostgreSQL CASE expression. ZeroHitRecordingService computes ZeroHitDemandSignals but only uses estimatedOpportunityLoss on the JPA path, while the aggregate recalculates priority internally. This split weakens locality of domain logic and raises drift risk.
findings.evidence: ZeroHitSearch.priorityFor() uses 5+/2+ thresholds; ZeroHitPriorityDecider.java:19-27 and ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway.java:52-56 repeat the same thresholds.
findings.suggestedFix: Choose one owner for priority rules. Prefer an aggregate method or a single domain policy, and make write paths delegate to that owner. Remove unused priority calculation from ZeroHitDemandSignals if the aggregate owns the rule.

findings.title: GET /api/products/search performs a database write when results are empty
findings.description: The search endpoint is exposed as GET, but its use case records or updates zero-hit demand whenever a non-empty search has no results. This violates the endpoint review rule that GET requests must be safe and side-effect free, and can be triggered by crawlers, retries, prefetching, or caches. The current repository spec also describes this behavior, so fixing it requires an API contract decision.
findings.evidence: `@GetMapping("/search")` delegates to `productSearchUseCase.search(...)`; `ProductSearchService.search` is `@Transactional` and calls `zeroHitRecordingService.record(trimmedKeyword)` when `totalCount == 0` at src/main/java/com/skishop/service/ProductSearchService.java:44 and :63-65. Integration tests assert the write at src/test/java/com/skishop/controller/ProductApiIntegrationTests.java:116-125.
findings.suggestedFix: Separate the read and write concerns. Keep `GET /api/products/search` safe, and record zero-hit demand through a state-changing POST endpoint such as `POST /api/products/search-events` or `POST /api/zero-hit-searches`. Update frontend calls, specs, and tests together. If the current behavior is intentionally retained, document the exception and add explicit no-store/cache controls, but it remains non-RESTful.

findings.title: Login request fields are not length-limited
findings.description: `LoginRequest` only uses `@NotBlank` for username and password. Unbounded credential strings are accepted by the controller and passed into authentication and the in-memory login limiter, including as part of the limiter key. External request DTO fields should have explicit maximum sizes to cap memory/CPU exposure and reject abusive payloads at the HTTP boundary.
findings.evidence: `public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank String username, @NotBlank String password)` has no `@Size` constraints, while `AuthController.login` correctly invokes validation with `@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest` at src/main/java/com/skishop/controller/AuthController.java:38.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit bounds, for example `@Size(max = 255)` on `username` and `@Size(min = 1, max = 256)` or another documented cap on `password`, then add controller tests proving overlong values return `400` with `VALIDATION_ERROR`.

findings.title: Current-user endpoint binds raw Authentication instead of an explicit principal
findings.description: `GET /api/auth/me` receives the framework `Authentication` object and casts `authentication.getPrincipal()` to `AdminUserDto`. The endpoint is protected by Spring Security, so this is not an observed IDOR bug, but the review standard prefers explicit `@AuthenticationPrincipal` binding for current-user resources. Explicit binding makes the endpoint contract clearer and avoids brittle casts if another authentication provider is introduced.
findings.evidence: `public AuthMeResponse me(Authentication authentication)` followed by `AdminUserDto user = (AdminUserDto) authentication.getPrincipal();`.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the method to bind the configured principal directly, e.g. `public AuthMeResponse me(@AuthenticationPrincipal AdminUserDto user)`, and keep token access for logout isolated where credentials are actually needed.

findings.title: Spring service is injected by concrete class without a corresponding interface
findings.description: The standards require Service classes to have corresponding interfaces and for consumers to depend on those abstractions. `ZeroHitRecordingService` is a Spring `@Service`, but it does not implement a use-case/interface and `ProductSearchService` injects the concrete class directly.
findings.evidence: private final ZeroHitRecordingService zeroHitRecordingService; ... ProductSearchService(... ZeroHitRecordingService zeroHitRecordingService)
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce an interface such as `ZeroHitRecordingUseCase` with `ZeroHitSearch record(String keyword)`, have `ZeroHitRecordingService implements ZeroHitRecordingUseCase`, and inject the interface in `ProductSearchService`.

findings.title: Repository/gateway component has no interface boundary
findings.description: `ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway` is annotated as `@Repository` but is only available as a concrete class. The standards require Repository classes to have corresponding interfaces; this also keeps database-specific PostgreSQL upsert details behind a replaceable boundary.
findings.evidence:
@Repository
public class ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway {
findings.suggestedFix: Create an interface such as `ZeroHitUpsertGateway` exposing `supportsAtomicUpsert()` and `upsert(...)`, implement it in `ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway`, and inject the interface into `ZeroHitRecordingService`.

findings.title: Nullable collection contract is implicit instead of annotated or normalized
findings.description: `AiPromptContext` collection components are declared as plain `List<String>`, while production code accepts null lists (`formatList` checks `values == null`) and tests construct `new AiPromptContext(null, null)`. The standards require `@Nullable`/`@NonNull` annotations where nullability is ambiguous, and collection contracts should avoid implicit null acceptance.
findings.suggestedFix: Prefer a compact constructor that normalizes null components to `List.of()` and copies non-null lists, then remove nullable handling from callers. If null must remain valid, annotate the record components and helper parameters with `@Nullable`.

findings.title: Intrinsic lock wraps JDBC metadata I/O during zero-hit upsert capability detection
findings.description: `supportsAtomicUpsert()` enters `synchronized (this)` and then calls `databaseProductName()`, which obtains a JDBC connection and reads metadata. If virtual threads are enabled as required for Java 21 adoption, this synchronized I/O can pin carrier threads. Even without virtual threads, first zero-hit requests serialize behind a monitor while waiting on the database.
findings.evidence: synchronized (this) { if (atomicUpsertSupported == null) { atomicUpsertSupported = databaseProductName().contains(POSTGRESQL); } } with databaseProductName() opening a JDBC connection at line 106.
findings.suggestedFix: Do not perform JDBC I/O inside an intrinsic monitor. Compute database support outside the lock and publish with an `AtomicReference<Boolean>`/volatile compare pattern, or initialize this once at startup in a bean lifecycle method without request-path monitor contention.

findings.title: Zero-hit JPA fallback serializes database reads and writes inside synchronized block
findings.description: The non-PostgreSQL fallback path wraps repository lookup and insert/update work in `synchronized (fallbackUpsertLock)`. Those calls perform database I/O and are reachable from `/api/products/search` when a zero-hit keyword is recorded. This pins virtual-thread carriers if Loom is enabled and serializes all fallback zero-hit writes across all keywords.
findings.evidence: synchronized (fallbackUpsertLock) { return zeroHitSearchRepository.findByNormalizedKeyword(normalizedKeyword).map(...).orElseGet(...); } and the mapped methods call `zeroHitSearchRepository.save(...)` at lines 101 and 115.
findings.suggestedFix: Avoid monitor-protected JPA I/O. Prefer database-native atomic upsert/MERGE for supported databases, pessimistic row locking plus unique-constraint retry, or a per-key `ReentrantLock` with clear cleanup if an application lock is unavoidable.

findings.title: Spring Boot virtual threads are not enabled
findings.description: The Java 21/Spring Boot service does not configure `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` in the main, Docker, or test application configuration. Under Spring MVC this keeps request handling on platform Tomcat threads, increasing thread-pool exhaustion risk for blocking database and AI provider work.
findings.evidence: `application.yml` defines `spring.application`, datasource, JPA, Flyway, and AI settings but no `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`; `application-docker.yml` and `application-test.yml` also omit it.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` to the base application configuration after removing or replacing synchronized-over-I/O paths that would pin carrier threads.

findings.title: Admin AI consultation performs synchronous external provider call on servlet request thread
findings.description: `AiConsultController.consult()` returns synchronously and delegates to `SpringAiProviderClient.generate()`, which calls Spring AI via `chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content()`. With virtual threads disabled and no explicit timeout visible in the ChatClient setup, slow provider calls can occupy Tomcat request threads and fallback is only reached after the provider call throws.
findings.evidence: String answer = chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content();
findings.suggestedFix: Enable virtual threads for servlet request handling and configure bounded provider timeouts. If the endpoint must remain on platform threads, return an async type or offload to a bounded executor with cancellation/timeout handling and explicit exception mapping.

findings.title: Active admin token limit is enforced with non-atomic compound operations
findings.description: `AdminAuthService` stores sessions in a `ConcurrentHashMap`, but the max-active-token invariant is enforced by a separate count/remove sequence before a later `put`. Concurrent successful logins for the same admin can all observe the same active count and then insert tokens, exceeding `MAX_ACTIVE_TOKENS_PER_ADMIN`. The map is thread-safe, but the multi-step invariant is not.
findings.evidence: `issueToken()` calls `enforceActiveTokenLimit(user)` at line 126, then inserts with `sessions.put(...)` at line 132; `enforceActiveTokenLimit()` counts and removes via streams at lines 137-146 without atomicity across the subsequent put.
findings.suggestedFix: Guard limit enforcement and insertion with a per-admin lock or redesign storage so updates for one admin happen atomically, for example a user-keyed session collection updated via `compute`.

findings.title: Requests do not get a correlation ID or MDC context
findings.description: No filter/interceptor reads or generates X-Correlation-Id, writes it to MDC, returns it in the response header, or clears MDC after the request. Request logs therefore cannot be reliably joined across services or even across layers during incident response.
findings.evidence: RequestLoggingFilter only records method, path, status, and duration. Repository-wide search found no MDC, correlationId, or X-Correlation-Id usage.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a OncePerRequestFilter that validates or generates X-Correlation-Id, calls MDC.put("correlationId", value), sets the response header, invokes the chain, and clears MDC in finally. Include correlationId in the JSON log pattern.

findings.title: Global exception responses are not RFC 7807 ProblemDetail
findings.description: The global handler and security error writer return a custom ApiErrorResponse with application/json instead of Spring Boot 3.2 ProblemDetail/application/problem+json. This fails the review requirement for RFC 7807/RFC 9457-compatible error payloads and makes exception-to-status mapping less standard for clients and tools.
findings.evidence: Every @ExceptionHandler returns ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse>; ApiErrorWriter creates ApiErrorResponse and sets MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE.
findings.suggestedFix: Return ProblemDetail from @ExceptionHandler methods using ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(...), set title/type/instance, and add validation details as properties. Update ApiErrorWriter to write ProblemDetail with application/problem+json and update frontend/tests together.

findings.title: Catch-all handler drops the exception stack trace
findings.description: The unexpected-exception handler logs only the path and exception class name. Because the Throwable is not passed to SLF4J, the server log loses the stack trace and causal chain exactly when it is most needed.
findings.evidence: LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error at {} with type {}", request.getRequestURI(), exception.getClass().getName());
findings.suggestedFix: Use placeholder logging with the Throwable as the final argument, e.g. LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error path={} type={}", request.getRequestURI(), exception.getClass().getName(), exception);

findings.title: AI provider failures are handled without logging the cause
findings.description: AiProviderException is caught and converted to a fallback response, but the catch block logs only providerStatus=ERROR. The provider exception and root cause are not recorded, which makes provider outages, timeouts, quota failures, and SDK failures hard to diagnose.
findings.evidence: catch (AiProviderException exception) { ... LOGGER.warn("ai_consultation providerStatus={}", response.providerStatus()); return response; }
findings.suggestedFix: Log a safe structured warning with the exception as the last argument, without prompt/user text: LOGGER.warn("ai_consultation providerStatus={} failureType={}", response.providerStatus(), exception.getClass().getName(), exception);

findings.title: Production JSON Logback configuration is missing
findings.description: The project uses SLF4J placeholders correctly, but there is no logback-spring.xml and no logstash-logback-encoder dependency. Production logs will be plain text by default, which weakens structured querying and also prevents MDC correlation IDs from being consistently emitted.
findings.evidence: The dependency list includes Spring Boot starters, Flyway, Spring AI, H2/PostgreSQL, and tests, but no logstash-logback-encoder. src/main/resources contains application.yml and application-docker.yml only; no logback-spring.xml was found.
findings.suggestedFix: Add net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder and src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml with JSON appenders including timestamp, level, logger, message, application name, correlationId, and trace/span IDs when available.

findings.title: Actuator metrics are not exposed and no business metrics are registered
findings.description: spring-boot-starter-actuator is present, but application.yml exposes only health. No MeterRegistry usage was found for key operational events such as zero-hit recording, AI provider status, or authentication failures. This leaves operators without basic runtime counters for the main demo workflows.
findings.evidence: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include is set to health only. Repository-wide search found no MeterRegistry, Counter, Timer, Gauge, Observation, or Tracer usage.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose metrics through a protected/internal path as appropriate, and add Micrometer counters/timers for zero_hit_recorded, ai_consultation providerStatus, auth failures, request latency, and provider failures.

findings.title: Shipping config contains hardcoded JDBC URL defaults
findings.description: The base and Docker datasource URLs include concrete PostgreSQL JDBC URLs as fallback values. The review standard requires JDBC URLs to come from environment variables or explicit Spring profiles, because fallback connection strings can accidentally be used outside local development.
findings.evidence: url: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/skishop}; application-docker.yml also defaults to jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/skishop
findings.suggestedFix: Remove JDBC URL defaults from the base profile, use `url: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL}` for deployable configs, and keep local/demo defaults only in a clearly named local profile or compose file.

findings.title: Native upsert path uses java.sql.Timestamp
findings.description: `java.sql.Timestamp` is prohibited by the data access standard. The gateway converts `Instant` to `Timestamp` for SQL binding, reintroducing legacy date/time API behavior in the persistence layer.
findings.evidence: import java.sql.Timestamp; ... "searchedAt", Timestamp.from(searchedAt)
findings.suggestedFix: Bind a java.time value directly, for example `OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(searchedAt, ZoneOffset.UTC)`, and align the migration column type if TIMESTAMPTZ semantics are intended.

findings.title: Product entity omits explicit snake_case column names
findings.description: Several `Product` fields rely on implicit column naming. The standard requires every persisted field to declare `@Column(name = "snake_case")` explicitly, including simple names such as `id`, `name`, and `price`.
findings.evidence: @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false) private UUID id; @Column(nullable = false) private String name;
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit names to every column, e.g. `@Column(name = "id", nullable = false, updatable = false)`, `@Column(name = "name", nullable = false, length = 255)`, and equivalent names for all remaining fields.

findings.title: ZeroHitSearch entity omits explicit snake_case column names
findings.description: `ZeroHitSearch` also relies on implicit column names for `id`, `keyword`, and `priority`. This violates the explicit entity blueprint convention and makes naming strategy changes risky.
findings.evidence: @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false) private UUID id; @Column(nullable = false) private String keyword; @Column(nullable = false, length = 20) private Priority priority;
findings.suggestedFix: Declare `name` on all columns, e.g. `@Column(name = "id", ...)`, `@Column(name = "keyword", ...)`, and `@Column(name = "priority", ...)`.

findings.title: Entity lifecycle generates UUID primary keys instead of service-layer String UUIDs
findings.description: Both entities use `UUID` primary keys and generate missing IDs inside `@PrePersist`. The review standard requires String UUID primary keys generated in the service layer with `UUID.randomUUID().toString()` and no entity-side generation.
findings.evidence: private UUID id; ... if (id == null) { id = UUID.randomUUID(); }
findings.suggestedFix: Align the entity and migrations with the project convention: `String id` with `@Column(name = "id", length = 36)`, generate IDs before construction/save in the service layer, and remove entity-side UUID defaults.

findings.title: Audit timestamps use callbacks instead of Hibernate creation/update annotations
findings.description: `Product.createdAt` and `Product.updatedAt` are audit fields, but they are maintained through `@PrePersist` and `@PreUpdate` with `Instant.now()`. The standard requires `@CreationTimestamp` and `@UpdateTimestamp` for audit timestamps.
findings.evidence: @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false) private Instant createdAt; ... @PreUpdate void preUpdate() { updatedAt = Instant.now(); }
findings.suggestedFix: Use `@CreationTimestamp` on `createdAt` and `@UpdateTimestamp` on `updatedAt`, and remove manual audit timestamp mutation from lifecycle callbacks.

findings.title: Public zero-hit write method lacks a service transaction boundary
findings.description: `ZeroHitRecordingService.record()` is a public state-changing method but is not annotated with `@Transactional`. It is currently transactional only when called through `ProductSearchService`; direct calls execute the native upsert and follow-up repository read without an explicit service-level transaction boundary.
findings.evidence: public ZeroHitSearch record(String keyword) { ... zeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway.upsert(...) : transactionTemplate.execute(...) }
findings.suggestedFix: Annotate the write use case with `@Transactional`, or move the full upsert/read flow behind one transactional gateway method with a clearly enforced propagation rule.

findings.title: ZeroHitSearch has concurrent update risk but no @Version column
findings.description: `ZeroHitSearch` stores mutable aggregate counters (`hitCount`, priority, opportunity loss). PostgreSQL atomic upsert covers the main path, but the JPA fallback updates the entity without optimistic locking and would not protect multi-instance fallback writes.
findings.evidence: Mutable fields `hitCount`, `priority`, `estimatedOpportunityLoss`, and `lastSearchedAt` exist, but no `@Version` field is declared.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `@Version @Column(name = "version") private Long version;` with a Flyway migration, and ensure the native upsert increments or returns the version consistently if the entity remains mutable through JPA.

findings.title: Docker profile ships a literal datasource password fallback
findings.description: `application-docker.yml` starts with a known database password when `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` is not supplied. The review standard has zero tolerance for literal password defaults in application configuration because a Docker/demo deployment can silently run with public credentials.
findings.evidence: password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the literal fallback and require an external value, for example `password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD}`. Put non-secret setup guidance in `.env.example` or Docker documentation, not in runtime config defaults.

findings.title: Authentication singletons keep mutable in-memory state
findings.description: `AdminAuthService` is a singleton `@Service` but owns mutable token/session state and sequencing fields. `InMemoryLoginAttemptLimiter` similarly owns mutable attempt state. Although concurrent collections are used, the token limit logic counts/removes/puts across separate operations, so concurrent logins can violate the intended active-token cap; the state is also process-local and lost across restarts or multiple instances. Under this agent’s criteria, singleton services must not hold mutable shared authentication state.
findings.evidence: @Service ... private final SecureRandom secureRandom = new SecureRandom(); private final Map<String, AdminSession> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final AtomicLong sessionSequence = new AtomicLong();
findings.suggestedFix: Move token/session and login-attempt state to a dedicated persistent or distributed store with atomic operations, or at minimum isolate it behind a state-store component with synchronized/atomic issue-and-limit semantics, bounded cleanup, and concurrency tests.

findings.title: Security headers are not explicitly configured
findings.description: The `SecurityFilterChain` does not call `headers(...)`. The required review perspective expects explicit security header configuration, including content type options, frame options, CSP, and HSTS where HTTPS is active. Spring defaults do not provide an explicit CSP policy and make the intended production posture hard to verify.
findings.evidence: The chain configures csrf, cors, sessionManagement, authorizeHttpRequests, exceptionHandling, disables httpBasic/formLogin/logout, and adds the bearer filter, but has no `.headers(...)` block.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an explicit headers block, for example `headers -> headers.contentTypeOptions(...).frameOptions(frame -> frame.deny()).contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> ...).httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> ...)`, with HSTS enabled for production HTTPS.

findings.title: Filter-chain DSL order does not follow the mandated order
findings.description: The mandated order requires CORS before CSRF/session/authorization and authentication filter configuration before headers. The implementation calls `csrf(...)` before `cors(...)`, and the bearer authentication filter is declared after authorization and login/logout config. Spring Security may still place filters by internal order, but the source configuration does not follow the explicit standard for this review agent.
findings.evidence: `.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)` appears on line 57, `.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` on line 58, `authorizeHttpRequests(...)` starts on line 60, and `.addFilterBefore(...)` is on line 80.
findings.suggestedFix: Reorder the DSL to the required sequence: `cors(...)`, `csrf(...)`, `sessionManagement(...)`, `authorizeHttpRequests(...)`, authentication provider/JWT filter registration, then `headers(...)`.

findings.title: Development and production profile files are missing
findings.description: Only `application.yml` and `application-docker.yml` exist under `src/main/resources`. There is no `application-dev.yml` or `application-prod.yml`, so production-specific logging levels, HTTPS/termination assumptions, and security overrides cannot be reviewed or enforced separately from common defaults.
findings.evidence: Resource scan found only `src/main/resources/application.yml` and `src/main/resources/application-docker.yml`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit `application-dev.yml` and `application-prod.yml`. Keep common safe defaults in `application.yml`; put dev-only relaxed logging/CORS in dev and production root logging, CORS origins, secret requirements, and HTTPS/reverse-proxy assumptions in prod.

findings.title: ConfigurationProperties records lack validation
findings.description: The project uses `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`, which is good, but the configuration records are not annotated with `@Validated` and do not define constraints. Blank/null admin credentials, invalid token TTLs, blank AI model names, or wildcard/null CORS origins can reach runtime configuration without startup validation.
findings.evidence: `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.admin") public record AdminProperties(String username, String password, Duration tokenTtl)`; similar unvalidated records exist for `AiProperties` and `CorsProperties`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `@Validated` and Bean Validation annotations, such as `@NotBlank` for required prod credentials/model values, `@NotNull`/duration bounds for token TTL, and CORS origin validation that rejects wildcard origins in production.

findings.title: No profile-aware Logback configuration is present
findings.description: The required security settings include `logback-spring.xml` with structured logging and profile-specific appenders. No such file exists in `src/main/resources`, and there are no profile-specific production log level settings in the application config files found.
findings.evidence: Resource scan found no `logback-spring.xml`; grep found no `logging:` configuration in main resources.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml` or explicit profile logging configuration. Set production root logging to WARN or above and ensure logs avoid secrets, tokens, and PII.

findings.title: Docker profile ships a hardcoded database password fallback
findings.description: The Docker profile falls back to a literal database password (`skishop`). If this profile is reused outside a local demo, deployments can come up with a known credential. The project standard has zero tolerance for hardcoded passwords or connection secrets.
findings.evidence: password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the literal fallback and require `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` at startup, or keep only non-secret sample values in an example file. Add startup validation that rejects blank/default production credentials.

findings.category: D Denial of Service / T Tampering / Business Logic Abuse
findings.title: Public GET search endpoint performs unauthenticated database writes with no rate limit
findings.description: `GET /api/products/search` is explicitly public and records a zero-hit row whenever a distinct non-empty query returns no products. An attacker can send many unique search terms to fill `zero_hit_searches`, pollute admin demand analytics, and consume database storage. Because it is a GET, this side effect can also be triggered by simple cross-site resource loads.
findings.suggestedFix: Add rate limiting to public search recording, cap total zero-hit rows per source/time window, add cleanup/retention, and consider moving recording to a POST endpoint or server-side telemetry pipeline. At minimum, throttle by trusted client identity and normalized keyword and reject high-cardinality abuse.

findings.title: Login rate limiting can be bypassed by spoofing X-Forwarded-For
findings.description: The login controller trusts `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` directly from the request and passes that value into the limiter key. A direct client can rotate these headers and avoid the per-username/per-IP lockout, enabling credential stuffing against the admin login.
findings.suggestedFix: Only honor forwarding headers when the immediate remote address is a trusted proxy, or use container/proxy-managed `ForwardedHeaderFilter` with trusted proxy configuration. Add a username-only or global limiter so IP rotation cannot reset the failure budget.

findings.category: Security Headers / A07 XSS Defense in Depth
findings.title: CSP, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and server header suppression are not configured
findings.description: The Spring Security chain relies on defaults and does not configure a Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy, or Permissions-Policy. `application.yml` also does not suppress the `Server` header. This weakens XSS containment and information disclosure defenses.
findings.evidence: The filter chain configures csrf/cors/session/auth/exception handling but has no `.headers(...)` block for CSP, referrer policy, permissions policy, or HSTS customization.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit security headers, for example `.headers(headers -> headers.contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'"))...)`, add referrer and permissions policies, and set `server.server-header=` in configuration.

findings.title: JSON request bodies are not globally size-limited
findings.description: The configuration limits headers and form posts, but the protected JSON endpoints use `@RequestBody`; Tomcat's form post size does not provide a general JSON body limit before Jackson parsing. Attackers can send oversized JSON bodies to login or admin endpoints and consume request parsing memory/CPU before Bean Validation runs.
findings.evidence: server.max-http-request-header-size and server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size are configured, but there is no generic request body limiting filter for application/json.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a servlet filter that rejects requests over a small maximum `Content-Length` for JSON APIs and fails chunked/unknown-length bodies beyond the cap, or enforce equivalent limits at the reverse proxy/gateway and document them as required production controls.

findings.title: Admin username can be inferred through timing differences
findings.description: The credential check short-circuits before password verification when the username is wrong. A wrong username avoids the password hash verification path, while the valid username path runs `passwordEncoder.matches`, creating a measurable timing difference that can reveal the configured admin username.
findings.evidence:
|| !adminProperties.username().equals(username)
|| !passwordEncoder.matches(password, adminProperties.password())
findings.suggestedFix: Always run password verification against either the real encoded password or a constant dummy hash, then combine the username/password results before returning the unified authentication failure.

findings.title: Production password encoder accepts `{noop}` admin passwords
findings.description: The production `PasswordEncoder` is `PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()`, which supports `{noop}`. The code comment says `{noop}` is for local tests, but there is no runtime guard preventing plaintext admin password configuration in non-test profiles.
findings.evidence:
Supports encoded admin passwords such as `{bcrypt}...` and `{noop}...` for local tests.
return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
findings.suggestedFix: Validate `app.admin.password` during startup and reject `{noop}` outside the `test` profile. Prefer `{bcrypt}` or another adaptive encoder for all deployable profiles.

findings.title: H2 is declared as a runtime dependency instead of test-only
findings.description: The POM exposes com.h2database:h2 with runtime scope even though the only detected configuration using H2 is the test profile. This violates the checklist requirement that H2 and other test-only dependencies use test scope, and it can accidentally place an in-memory database driver on the production runtime classpath.
findings.evidence: pom.xml declares com.h2database:h2 with <scope>runtime</scope>; src/test/resources/application-test.yml uses jdbc:h2 and org.h2.Driver.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the H2 dependency scope to test unless a documented production/local runtime profile genuinely requires it.

findings.title: Required structured logging dependency is missing
findings.description: The dependency checklist requires net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder for logging, but the dependencies block does not declare it. Without it, the backend cannot emit Logback JSON/structured logs through the required encoder.
findings.evidence: The dependencies block includes Spring Boot starters, Flyway, Spring AI, H2, PostgreSQL, and test dependencies, but no net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder entry.
findings.suggestedFix: Add net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder with an approved stable version, or document a project-level decision changing the required logging standard.

findings.title: Maven encoding properties are not declared
findings.description: The required build configuration expects project.build.sourceEncoding and project.reporting.outputEncoding to be UTF-8. The POM only declares java.version, flyway.version, and jacoco.version, so Maven plugin behavior may fall back to environment defaults.
findings.evidence: <properties> contains java.version, flyway.version, and jacoco.version only.
findings.suggestedFix: Add <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> and <project.reporting.outputEncoding>UTF-8</project.reporting.outputEncoding>.

findings.title: Flyway version overrides Spring Boot's managed dependency set
findings.description: The POM overrides flyway.version to 10.22.0 while using spring-boot-starter-parent 3.2.12. This bypasses the parent BOM's tested Flyway version set and should be justified because the review standard requires Spring-managed dependency versions to be inherited from the parent where possible.
findings.evidence: pom.xml sets <flyway.version>10.22.0</flyway.version> and uses that property on flyway-database-postgresql at line 73.
findings.suggestedFix: Prefer the Spring Boot parent-managed Flyway version, or upgrade the Spring Boot parent to a compatible line that manages the required Flyway module/version. If the override is intentional, document the compatibility rationale and keep Flyway artifacts aligned.

findings.title: POM license metadata is empty
findings.description: The POM contains an empty <license/> element. For OSS publication and downstream dependency consumers, Maven coordinates should declare the selected project license explicitly.
findings.evidence: <licenses><license/></licenses> is present without name or URL.
findings.suggestedFix: Populate the license metadata after the project owner selects the OSS license, for example name and URL for MIT, Apache-2.0, or the chosen license.

findings.title: All test methods violate required should_ExpectedResult_when_Condition pattern
findings.description: The suite uses descriptive prose method names, but the active review standard requires every test method to use the camelCase `should_ExpectedResult_when_Condition` pattern. `rg` found 77 `@Test` methods and none with the required `should_` prefix/pattern.
findings.evidence: Representative names include `keywordNormalizerTrimsLowercasesAndCollapsesWhitespace`, `validLoginReturnsTokenAndAdminUser`, and `productRepositorySupportsInitialListSearchAverageAndAiContextQueries`; none follow `should_X_when_Y`.
findings.suggestedFix: Rename tests to specification-style names, e.g. `should_returnNormalizedKeyword_when_keywordHasMixedCaseAndWhitespace`, `should_returnTokenAndAdminUser_when_credentialsAreValid`, and `should_returnProductsAndAiContext_when_repositoryQueriesAreCalled`.

findings.title: No tests use @DisplayName for human-readable specifications
findings.description: The review standard expects `@DisplayName` for readable descriptions. The test tree contains no `@DisplayName` annotations, so reports will rely entirely on method names that already violate the required naming convention.
findings.evidence: `rg -n "@DisplayName" src/test/java` returned no matches; representative test starts at `@Test` then method declaration without a display name.
findings.suggestedFix: Add concise `@DisplayName` values above tests, especially API and domain tests, while also renaming methods to the required pattern.

findings.title: Several tests combine multiple acts and behaviors without clear AAA separation
findings.description: Some tests execute multiple production calls and assertions in a single method without Arrange / Act / Assert comments or clear one-act structure. This makes failures harder to diagnose and violates the review agent's act-singularity requirement.
findings.evidence: `toPageableUsesDefaultsAndAllowedSorts` performs four separate `ProductRequestOptions.toPageable(...)` calls and asserts default behavior plus three sort variants in one test method.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into focused tests such as `should_useDefaultLimitAndSort_when_optionsAreMissing` and parameterized sort tests like `should_returnAllowedSort_when_sortTokenIsSupported`, each with explicit Arrange / Act / Assert blocks.

findings.title: Repeated boundary/error matrices are not parameterized
findings.description: The suite has repeated boundary and invalid-input assertions but does not use `@ParameterizedTest`, `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource`, or `@MethodSource`. This reduces readability and makes it easier to miss individual cases in reports.
findings.evidence: `toPageableRejectsInvalidLimitAndSort` checks limit 0, limit 101, and invalid sort as repeated assertions; `rg` found no parameterized-test annotations anywhere under `src/test/java`.
findings.suggestedFix: Convert repeated input matrices to parameterized tests, for example `should_throwIllegalArgumentException_when_limitIsOutsideAllowedRange(Integer limit)` with `@ValueSource(ints = {0, 101})`.

findings.title: Controller branch coverage is below the required 80% target
findings.description: The existing JaCoCo report shows controller package branch coverage at 50% because `AuthController` has 5 missed and 5 covered branches. This fails the controller layer branch coverage target of 80%+.
findings.evidence: `target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv` reports `AuthController` with `BRANCH_MISSED=5` and `BRANCH_COVERED=5`; package aggregation is 5/10 branches = 50%. Branches correspond to logout credential null handling and `sourceIp` header selection paths.
findings.suggestedFix: Add MockMvc tests that cover `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, remote-address fallback, and logout credential-null behavior where reachable, or refactor source IP extraction into a public/testable collaborator with focused unit tests.

findings.title: Public 404 handler is uncovered
findings.description: The public `GlobalExceptionHandler.handleNotFound` method has no coverage in the JaCoCo report, violating the requirement that all public methods be tested.
findings.evidence: JaCoCo marks `handleNotFound` at line 109 as `METHOD missed=1 covered=0`; there is no API test asserting the controlled 404 payload for an unknown route.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a MockMvc integration test such as `should_returnNotFoundPayload_when_pathDoesNotExist` that requests an unmapped route and asserts status 404 plus `code == NOT_FOUND`.

findings.title: Coverage thresholds are reported but not enforced by Maven
findings.description: `jacoco-maven-plugin` is configured for `prepare-agent` and `report`, but there is no `check` execution with line/branch minimums. A future regression below 80% would still pass Maven unless reviewers inspect the report manually.
findings.evidence: The plugin executions include only `prepare-agent` and `report`; no `jacoco:check` rule exists for line or branch coverage minimums.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a `check` execution in `verify` with rules enforcing at least 0.80 line and branch coverage, with any deliberate exclusions documented.

findings.title: Collection APIs expose only a limit and always return the first page
findings.description: The product list, product search, and admin zero-hit list endpoints accept only `limit`; `ProductRequestOptions` hard-codes `PageRequest.of(0, safeLimit, ...)`. This bounds each response but is not real pagination: clients cannot request later pages and responses do not include page/size metadata. Under a larger catalog or radar table, users either see only the first slice or require new API behavior.
findings.evidence: `toPageable` validates `limit` and returns `PageRequest.of(0, safeLimit, toSort(sort))`; controllers expose `limit` but no `page` parameter in `ProductController` lines 40-58 and `AdminZeroHitController` lines 38-42.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `page` and `size` request parameters with defaults and max size, return pagination metadata (`page`, `size`, `totalElements`, `totalPages`), and map from `Page<T>` to DTOs, e.g. `PageRequest.of(page, cappedSize, sort)` plus a paged response record.

findings.title: Zero-hit summary scans the same filtered rows three times
findings.description: `listZeroHits` calculates summary cards by executing separate count, hit-count sum, and opportunity-loss sum queries with the same `lastSearchedAt >= :since` predicate. This repeats work on the radar table every admin dashboard load and grows worse as zero-hit history grows.
findings.evidence: `countRadarItems(since)`, `sumHitCount(since)`, and `sumEstimatedOpportunityLoss(since)` are called consecutively; repository queries at `ZeroHitSearchRepository` lines 39-64 use the same filter.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the three repository calls with one aggregate projection query, e.g. `select new com.skishop.dto.ZeroHitSummaryDto(count(z), coalesce(sum(z.hitCount),0), coalesce(sum(z.estimatedOpportunityLoss),0)) from ZeroHitSearch z where z.lastSearchedAt >= :since`.

findings.title: Product keyword search is non-sargable and cannot use the existing indexes effectively
findings.description: Keyword search lowercases multiple columns and uses leading-wildcard `LIKE` patterns. The migration creates ordinary btree indexes on `name`, `manufacturer`, and `category`, which do not support `lower(column) LIKE '%term%'` well. Product search is a primary user path, so this will trend toward full scans as the catalog grows.
findings.evidence: `String pattern = "%" + ... + "%"` and `criteriaBuilder.like(criteriaBuilder.lower(root.get(...)), pattern)` are used; migration `V1__create_products_and_zero_hit_searches.sql` lines 30-32 creates plain indexes, not functional/trigram/full-text indexes.
findings.suggestedFix: Measure with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` at expected catalog size, then use a PostgreSQL search strategy such as `pg_trgm` GIN indexes on normalized text, full-text search with a generated `tsvector`, or prefix-only search if substring search is not required.

findings.title: Stable product master context is queried on every AI consultation
findings.description: AI consultation fetches distinct product categories and manufacturers for every request. These values are product master data and likely change rarely, but no Spring Cache, Redis, or equivalent cache layer is configured. This adds avoidable DB reads to every admin AI call.
findings.evidence: The service constructs `AiPromptContext` from `productRepository.findDistinctCategories()` and `findDistinctManufacturers()` on each call; repository methods are defined at `ProductRepository` lines 60-67, and no `@Cacheable`/cache dependency was found.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce Spring Cache for product master lookups, for example `@Cacheable("productCategories")` and `@Cacheable("productManufacturers")`, and add `@CacheEvict` when future admin product updates are introduced.

findings.title: Login attempt limiter keeps failed-attempt keys indefinitely
findings.description: The in-memory limiter stores failed login state in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and only removes entries on successful login. Expired windows are overwritten only if the same key appears again, so a long-running process receiving many unique username/IP combinations can accumulate stale entries indefinitely.
findings.evidence: `attempts` is an unbounded `ConcurrentHashMap`; `recordFailure` updates entries, while `recordSuccess` is the only removal path.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a bounded/expiring cache such as Caffeine (`maximumSize`, `expireAfterWrite`) or add scheduled cleanup of entries whose window and lock have expired.

findings.title: Prompt list formatting creates an intermediate list and concatenates strings in a reduce
findings.description: `formatList` maps values to strings, collects them to a list, streams again, then reduces with string concatenation. The list is capped at 20, so the current impact is small, but the same output can be produced with less allocation and clearer code.
findings.evidence: The pipeline uses `.toList().stream().reduce((left, right) -> left + System.lineSeparator() + right)`.
findings.suggestedFix: Use `Collectors.joining(System.lineSeparator())` directly after mapping, then return `"- なし"` when the joined result is blank.

findings.title: External AI provider call has no Resilience4j retry or circuit breaker
findings.description: The live external provider call is made through Spring AI ChatClient without @Retry, @CircuitBreaker, or equivalent resilience wrapper. pom.xml also has no Resilience4j or Spring Retry dependency/configuration, so transient provider failures are handled only after a single failed attempt and there is no circuit opening to prevent repeated failing calls.
findings.evidence: String answer = chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content(); followed by catch/rethrow as AiProviderException. Repository search found no @Retry, @CircuitBreaker, @TimeLimiter, @Bulkhead, resilience4j, or Retryable usage in src/main/pom.xml.
findings.suggestedFix: Add resilience4j-spring-boot3 (or Spring Retry), configure app.ai/provider retry with maxAttempts 3, exponential backoff, and circuit breaker thresholds, then annotate/wrap generate(), for example @Retry(name="aiProvider", fallbackMethod="fallback") and @CircuitBreaker(name="aiProvider", fallbackMethod="fallback").

findings.title: Spring AI OpenAI client is created without an explicit timeout contract
findings.description: The OpenAiApi and ChatClient are manually constructed with only apiKey and model settings. No connect, read, response, or operation timeout is configured in code or application.yml for this external call path, so request latency is governed by library defaults rather than an explicit service contract.
findings.evidence: OpenAiApi.builder().apiKey(...).build(); OpenAiChatModel.builder().openAiApi(openAiApi)...build(); no timeout-related builder options or app.ai timeout properties are present.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose timeout settings under app.ai, configure the underlying Spring AI/OpenAI HTTP client with connect/read/response timeouts, and optionally add a Resilience4j TimeLimiter around the provider operation.

findings.title: No custom health indicator for the live AI provider dependency
findings.description: Actuator health probes are enabled, but there is no HealthIndicator or readiness contributor for the external AI provider. When AI_API_KEY is configured, the app can silently degrade to providerStatus=ERROR while /actuator/health/readiness remains unrelated to provider availability.
findings.evidence: management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true exposes health probes, but repository search found no HealthIndicator, Readiness, Liveness, or Availability component for the AI provider.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an AI provider HealthIndicator or Availability state contributor. If live AI is optional, expose it as a named component/detail without gating core readiness; if it is critical for admin workflows, include it in readiness with a cheap bounded check.

findings.title: Graceful shutdown is not configured
findings.description: The server configuration omits server.shutdown=graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase. During deploys or container stops, in-flight requests can be interrupted instead of drained within a bounded shutdown window.
findings.evidence: The server block configures request/header/error settings but contains no shutdown setting; application-docker.yml also only sets server.port.
findings.suggestedFix: Configure server.shutdown=graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, for example 20s-30s, and align container termination grace periods with that value.

findings.title: No concurrency isolation for high-latency AI provider calls
findings.description: The admin AI consultation endpoint can call an external model provider from request handling without @Bulkhead or another concurrency limiter. A slow or degraded provider can consume servlet worker threads and affect unrelated backend APIs.
findings.evidence: The provider call is made synchronously through chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content(); repository search found no @Bulkhead or bulkhead configuration.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a Resilience4j semaphore bulkhead for the AI provider with a small maxConcurrentCalls value and a bounded wait duration, returning the existing provider error/fallback response when saturated.

escalations.description: docs/migration/DESIGN.md and PLAN.md referenced by the tech-lead agent definition were not present in the accessible repository tree. This review used AGENTS.md plus spec-design/zero-hit-radar-requirment.md and spec-design/backend-design.md instead.
Decide whether the project standard should use `model` or `entity` for JPA classes. The code consistently uses `entity`, while the architecture review checklist requires `model`.

The backend design document explicitly describes ProductSearchService calling ZeroHitRecordingService directly, while the DDD review standard requires event-driven inter-aggregate coordination. A human decision is needed on whether to revise the design toward events or accept the MVP coupling as intentional technical debt.

Decide whether the product search contract should remain `GET /api/products/search` with zero-hit recording, as currently specified, or be split into a safe GET plus a POST recording endpoint. This affects backend spec, frontend client behavior, and integration tests.

Decide whether non-PostgreSQL zero-hit recording is a production-supported path. If yes, replace the synchronized fallback with a database-safe atomic strategy before enabling virtual threads. If no, remove the fallback from production wiring and keep H2-only test support isolated.
Migrating ApiErrorResponse to ProblemDetail may affect frontend contracts and existing integration tests. Coordinate the API error contract update with the frontend and test owners.
Decide the operational policy for actuator metrics exposure: internal-only endpoint, authenticated admin endpoint, or Prometheus scrape endpoint behind infrastructure controls.

The codebase currently uses native PostgreSQL UUID columns while the review agent standard requires String UUID IDs. A maintainer should decide whether the agent standard or the existing schema design is authoritative before changing migrations and API DTO types.
Confirm whether Docker deployments are intended to be publishable OSS demos with default database credentials, or whether runtime secrets must be mandatory before startup.
Confirm where production HTTPS is terminated. No `server.ssl.*` configuration or production profile documentation was present in the reviewed backend target.
Decide whether the Docker profile is intended for deployable environments. If yes, the default DB password must be removed before OSS release.
Confirm the production proxy topology. If the app can receive direct traffic, forwarded headers must not be trusted for rate limiting.
Decide whether zero-hit recording should remain on a public GET endpoint or be moved behind a controlled telemetry/write path.
Project owner/legal decision is needed to choose and publish the intended OSS license before filling the POM license metadata.

Decide whether to apply the strict `should_ExpectedResult_when_Condition` naming rule retroactively to all 77 existing tests in one cleanup PR, since this is a broad mechanical change but required by the active review standard.
Decide whether the public/admin API contract should move from limit-only slices to page/size pagination before frontend contracts are frozen.
Set expected product catalog size and search latency target, then choose between trigram, full-text, or simpler prefix search based on measured query plans.

Decide whether live AI availability should gate readiness. The current product has fallback behavior, so SRE/product owners should choose between non-gating health visibility and readiness failure when AI is unavailable.
